name: The Ski Rental Problem
statement: Not knowing how long you'll keep skiing, rent until the rentals equal the purchase price, then buy.
statementAccent: rent until the rentals equal the purchase price
meaning: The ski rental problem is the archetypal rent-or-buy decision under uncertainty, the canonical example of online algorithms and competitive analysis. You will ski for an unknown number of days; each day you can rent skis for a dollar, or at any point buy them once for some larger amount and ski free thereafter, but you never know when the season will end. The goal is to keep your total cost close to what you would have paid with perfect hindsight. The problem crisply captures a whole family of wait-versus-commit choices, and its clean answer illustrates how to reason about decisions made without knowledge of the future.
mechanism: The classic strategy is to break even: rent until the money spent on rentals equals the purchase price, then buy. This deterministic rule is two-competitive, meaning its cost never exceeds twice the best possible cost in hindsight. The worst case is that the season ends the very day you buy, so you have paid the purchase price in rentals plus the purchase price again, about twice the optimum. An online algorithm is called c-competitive if, on every input, its cost is at most c times the offline optimum, a worst-case guarantee against an adversary, not an average. Introducing randomness improves the ratio to about 1.58, which is provably the best any randomized strategy can achieve.

examples.text: If skis cost ten dollars to buy, rent for nine days and buy on the tenth; the worst case costs nineteen dollars against an optimum of ten, a ratio of 1.9.
Deciding whether to send an acknowledgement now or wait to batch several is a direct generalisation of the rent-or-buy tradeoff, the TCP acknowledgement problem.
The two-cache, one-block cache-coherence problem is mathematically equivalent to ski rental, the setting in which the rent-or-buy analysis first arose.

variants.name: The randomised strategy
variants.text: Buying on a random day drawn from a carefully chosen distribution lowers the competitive ratio to about 1.58, the optimum against an oblivious adversary.

variants.name: Learning-augmented ski rental
variants.text: Modern variants that give the algorithm a prediction of the season length, blending worst-case guarantees with machine-learned advice.

whyItMatters: The ski rental problem is the standard teaching example of online algorithms and competitive analysis, the study of decisions made without knowledge of the future measured against the best possible hindsight. Its simple break-even rule and two-competitive guarantee model a vast range of real wait-versus-commit tradeoffs, from TCP acknowledgement batching and cache coherence to cloud resource provisioning and capacity planning. It shows how a provable worst-case guarantee can be extracted from an apparently hopeless situation, and it opened a rich line of work, including randomised and learning-augmented strategies, in the theory of decision-making under uncertainty.

working.text: keep renting until your rental spending equals the purchase price, then buy, the deterministic two-competitive rule.
judge an online strategy by its competitive ratio, the worst-case factor by which it exceeds the best cost achievable with foreknowledge.
when possible, buy on a randomly chosen day to lower the competitive ratio toward the optimal one over one minus one over e, about 1.58.

limits: The clean ratios are asymptotic: the deterministic optimum is two minus one over the purchase price, approaching two for large prices, and the randomised optimum of about 1.58 also holds in the limit. The randomised bound assumes an oblivious adversary that fixes the input without seeing the algorithm's coin flips; against an adaptive adversary randomness gives no advantage and the ratio returns to two. The model assumes a known constant buy cost and linearly accruing rentals, and competitive analysis is deliberately pessimistic, worst-case over all inputs, which motivated later average-case and prediction-augmented refinements.
misreadings: A competitive ratio is a worst-case guarantee against the hindsight optimum, not an average or expected performance. Two-competitive does not mean the strategy costs twice as much as renting or buying; it means at most twice the best possible cost, reached only in the single worst case where the season ends exactly at the break-even day. And the randomised strategy legitimately beats the deterministic lower bound because the adversary cannot predict the coin flips, so this is no contradiction.
origin: A canonical problem of online algorithms, arising from the rent-or-buy analysis of Karlin, Manasse, Rudolph, and Sleator's 1988 'Competitive Snoopy Caching', within the framework of competitive analysis introduced by Sleator and Tarjan in 1985.

sources.text: Ski rental problem, Wikipedia. — the rent-or-buy setup, the break-even two-competitive result, and the randomised optimum.
Karlin, Manasse, Rudolph & Sleator, 'Competitive Snoopy Caching,' Algorithmica (1988). — the rent-or-buy analysis equivalent to ski rental.
